cards.title: Memory is a terrible medical record
cards.body: 'It happens sometimes' doesn't help a doctor much. A simple diary turns vague worry into patterns that can actually be looked at.

cards.title: Why it helps the doctor
cards.body: Dates, times and triggers show whether a problem is getting better or worse, and whether it links to food, sleep or a new medicine.

cards.title: Keep it boring and short
cards.body: One line per entry: date, time, what happened, how long, how bad. A notebook by the bed or a note on the phone both work.

cards.title: Note what was happening around it
cards.body: Before or after meals, after medicine, after a walk, after a bad night's sleep. Context is where the patterns hide.

cards.title: Track medicines and missed doses too
cards.body: Write down if a dose was missed, taken late, or if a new tablet started. Doctors find this more useful than people expect.

cards.title: Bring it, but summarise it
cards.body: Show the diary at the visit with a three line summary on top. The doctor can scan the summary and dig deeper if needed.

cards.title: Make it a family habit
cards.body: Whoever is with Papa writes the entry and shares it with the family. AICA's care diary is built for this, but a notebook works too.

takeaway: A short daily symptom diary with times, triggers and medicine notes gives doctors patterns instead of guesses.
share: Start a symptom diary for Papa. Date, time, what happened, how bad. The doctor will thank you.
